checkins.m1_prediction: With too little Kp I expect the arm to move very slowly and not fully reach its end pose/target, while too little Kd would result in a very strong and bouncy arm. Where it will overshoot in terms of reaching the target and it would be hard to settle from that when trying to hold a target it will be very bouncy before it fully settles.
checkins.m1_arm_tuning: I predicted that low Kp would make the arm very slow and it wouldn't be able to get to the target, while low Kd would be too bouncy and have a lot of bounces before it could hold the target. My predictions were accurate the low Kp was extremely loose and weak and low Kd was bouncing all over the place never being able to stay in one position to hold the target. With low Kp and Kd it was unable to hold the target at any point. It was both a mix of overshooting and not being strong enough to hold its position.  However, when the kp and kd were closer in value the arm became a lot more stable. I'm not entirely sure what gravity compensation changed because I didn't really notice any strong changes/differences.
checkins.final_reflection: I enjoyed this lab because I got to manipulate the key parts of the robot that makes it move around in the real world. The simulation itself was cool and relatively easy to use. This made me wonder if our group would use this to help us figure out how we want our robot to behave and move around. Something that stood out to me was that a robot can return readings that are seemingly fine but in practice the robot is actually way off and that is due to a calibration error. There will be no immediate flag that something is wrong until it is seen in action, which is important to keep in mind when we are designing and building our robot.
